issues.legal_issue: A priest who holds temple land only to manage the deity’s property does not acquire Bhumiswami status merely because the land is associated with religious service.
material_facts: The land in dispute was temple land, and the priest’s role under the applicable historical arrangements was to manage the property and perform religious duties.
The priest could cultivate the land or have it cultivated for the temple’s upkeep, but did not hold it as an ordinary tenant or landholder with ownership rights.
The priest was not within the classes of landholders whose rights were protected as Bhumiswamis under the applicable land legislation.
issues.conclusion: A priest who manages temple land on behalf of the deity is not a Bhumiswami on that basis and has no ownership right in the temple land.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 158(1)(b) of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, 2007 and the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, specified classes of landholders could become Bhumiswamis; a priest holding land only to manage temple property does not fall within those classes. Section 57’s protection of existing rights does not create a proprietary right where none existed. Pancham Singh v. Ramkishandas Guru Ramdas held that a priest managing such land was not a tenant in cultivation or ordinary tenant; this Court approved that view in Mst. Kanchaniya v. Shiv Ram. M. Siddiq v. Mahant Suresh Das also supports the principle that performing worship does not by itself confer independent rights in religious property.

predicates.temple_land_belongs_to_deity: The land is held for a temple and belongs to the deity rather than to its priest.
predicates.priest_holds_land_only_for_management: The priest holds or manages the land on behalf of the deity to maintain the temple and perform its religious functions.
predicates.priest_is_not_an_ordinary_landholder: The priest does not hold the land in an ordinary tenant or other landholder capacity that carries the relevant land rights.

issues.definition: When temple land belongs to the deity and a priest holds it only to manage it, without an ordinary landholder status, the priest is not a Bhumiswami.

issues.legal_issue: Revenue records need not identify a priest or manager as owner or occupier of temple land, and executive instructions may regulate entries where legislation and rules do not require such identification.
material_facts: The applicable record-of-rights provisions and rules prescribed entries for land records, including the identity of an occupier and other prescribed particulars.
The deity owned the temple land, while any occupation or management by the priest was carried out as the deity’s servant or manager.
No provision or rule required the priest’s or a manager’s name to be entered in the ownership or occupancy columns.
The State issued instructions concerning the recording of priests’ names, including maintaining separate records of priests.
issues.conclusion: The deity’s name is to be recorded as owner; the priest’s name is not required in the ownership or occupancy columns, though it may be entered in the remarks column. Executive instructions supplementing the statute and rules are not illegal merely because they regulate such entries.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 108, 114, 121 and 258 of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, and the rules prescribing the khasra form govern land-record entries. The prescribed form distinguishes the occupier and other land interests from remarks. Because the deity owns the land and the rules do not require the priest or manager to be recorded as owner or occupier, the priest’s name is not mandatory in those columns, although it may be recorded in remarks. In the absence of a statutory or rule-based prohibition, executive instructions may supplement the governing framework. Ghanshyamdas II is consistent with the possibility of recording a priest’s name in the remarks column without affecting the priest’s managerial functions.

rule.if: temple_land_belongs_to_deity and priest_acts_only_as_manager and no_rule_requires_priest_entry and executive_instruction_supplements_recording_rules

predicates.temple_land_belongs_to_deity: The temple land belongs to the deity rather than to the priest or manager.
predicates.priest_acts_only_as_manager: The priest’s role in relation to the land is limited to managing it for the deity.
predicates.no_rule_requires_priest_entry: No applicable rule requires the priest’s name to be entered as owner or occupier.
predicates.executive_instruction_supplements_record: The government instruction regulates record entries without contradicting a statutory or rule-based requirement.

issues.definition: Where the deity owns the land, the priest acts only as manager, no rule requires the priest’s ownership or occupancy entry, and an instruction supplements the record rules, the priest’s name is not required in those columns.

issues.legal_issue: The Collector cannot be designated as manager in land records for temple property merely by a general executive instruction when the property is vested in the deity.
material_facts: The temple property was vested in the deity and was not shown to be vested in the State.
The State’s instructions contemplated recording the Collector as manager of temple property.
The Court found no basis for treating a Collector as manager of every temple, while recognising that a temple vested in the State could stand differently.
issues.conclusion: The Collector’s name cannot be recorded as manager of property vested in the deity merely under a general instruction; the position may differ where the temple is vested in the State.
issues.legal_principle: The deity is the owner of temple property, and a Collector is not the manager of every temple. The Court distinguished property vested in a deity from a temple vested in the State and relied on Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar for the distinction between public and private endowments. A general executive instruction cannot treat the Collector as manager of all deity-owned temple property.

predicates.temple_property_is_vested_in_deity: The property belongs to the deity and is not vested in the State.
predicates.collector_is_named_as_manager_by_general: A general government instruction directs that the Collector be recorded as manager of the temple property.
predicates.temple_is_not_vested_in_state: The temple property has not been shown to be vested in the State.

issues.definition: If deity-owned temple property is not vested in the State, a general instruction cannot make the Collector its recorded manager.

issues.legal_issue: Government instructions concerning temple land records apply to temples generally unless a particular temple establishes that it is private.
material_facts: The challenged instructions did not distinguish between public and private temples.
The Court observed that a temple in a house or one not open to the public cannot be treated as a public temple.
Whether a particular temple is public or private is a matter for determination in appropriate proceedings before the competent forum.
issues.conclusion: The instructions apply to temples unless a particular temple establishes before the competent forum that it is private.
issues.legal_principle: Whether an endowment is public or private depends on the purpose of the dedication and the intended beneficiaries. Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar explains that an endowment for specified individuals is private, while an endowment intended to benefit the general body of worshippers is public. The status of a particular temple is a question for the competent forum on the facts of that case.

predicates.temple_record_instruction_is_challenged: A party disputes the application of a government instruction concerning temple land records.
predicates.private_temple_status_has_not_been_estab: The particular temple has not established before a competent forum that it is private.

issues.definition: When a temple-record instruction is disputed but the temple has not established its private status, the instruction applies to it.
